newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian Socialist Nano confident of election win.
newsitem.headline: Albanian Socialist Nano confident of election win.

text.p: Socialist leader Fatos Nano said on Saturday that popular discontent with Albanian President Sali Berisha was so rife that his party would score a resounding victory in this month's parliamentary election.
However Nano expressed the hope that Berisha would cooperate with a future Socialist administration to build a market-based future for Europe's poorest country.

"Berisha has made many mistakes in five years in power. The majority of Albanians are protesting not against democracy but against misuse of democratic institutions which made them feel marginalised in their homeland," he said in English.

"The anti-Berisha protest is a very strong factor which will give victory absolutely to the opposition. The Socialists have massive support. We will not misuse that support and will create a coalition government of centre-left parties."
Berisha has been waging a high-profile campaign on behalf of his Democratic Party, which is defending a huge majority won in elections last May criticised as unfair in Albania and abroad.

The outcome of the new polls is virtually impossible to predict in a country with no real opinion polls and huge disparities between cities and the backward countryside. But Socialist rallies have drawn bigger crowds than Berisha's Democrats.
Anti-Berisha protests earlier this year pitched Albania into near-lawlessness after hundreds of thousands of people lost savings in collapsed investment schemes.
A 7,000-strong international peacekeeping force has been deployed, but some southern areas remain outside the control of authorities.

Berisha, a free-market advocate initially supported by Western countries but later widely accused of abusing his power, was obliged to appoint a multi-party government in March and agree to early election.

Nano, a former prime minister, was freed in March after four years in prison on fraud charges the opposition says were politically inspired. He said Berisha had little choice but to work with whatever government emerged from the elections.
"We have offered him the chance of forming a reconciliation government. He has a chance to make a new political reputation ...There is no alternative but for him to cooperate," he said.
"If Berisha says in the old way 'I'm not going to leave', I'm afraid on June 30 rats will start leaving the sinking ship."
Nano said he would be travelling to Rome on Monday to sign an accord with other party leaders -- organised by an Italian Roman Catholic peace group -- to ensure a smooth election.
But with just over a week to go, doubts persist on whether a free and fair vote is possible with armed gangs still at large in many parts of the rugged country of 3.4 million.
All but 40 of the 155 seats are to be decided in two-round majority contests, but officials were still debating how to decide the remaining seats under proportional representation.
All major parties have also agreed to close polling stations before nightfall to guard against violence and cheating, but the change must still secure legal approval.

Nano said a new Socialist government would quickly provide a legal framework to right the economy, encourage foreign investment and try to recover some of the estimated $1.2 billion that investors lost in the pyramid scheme collapses.

"We've got to confiscate every damned penny stolen from people in pyramid schemes or other forms of corruption. You will not find a thief anywhere in the world willing to compensate his victims voluntarily."

"We will urgently install what has already been set up, create economic stability and stabilise the currency," he said, adding that his government would work to adopt any measures suggested by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or World Bank.
